cues.text: ODYSSEY — BOOK X
Aeolus and the bag of winds;\nthe Laestrygonians; a year with Circe.
We came next to the Aeolian island; and there lived\nAeolus, Hippotas' son, dear to the deathless gods,
on a floating island: all around it a wall of bronze,\nunbreakable, and the cliff runs up sheer.
Twelve children of his live in his halls,\nsix daughters and six sons in their prime,
and he has given his daughters\nto his sons to be their wives.
They are always feasting beside their dear father
and their honored mother, and good\nthings past counting are set before them;
all day the house is savory with roasting,\nand the courtyard rings with the sound;
and at night they sleep beside their honored\nwives among blankets, on corded bedsteads.
To their city, then, we came, and their beautiful house.
A full month he made much of me,\nand questioned me on everything —
Ilium, the Argives' ships, the Achaeans' homecoming —\nand I told him all of it through, in its due order.
And when I in my turn asked for the road, and begged him
to send me on, he refused me nothing:\nhe prepared my sending.
He gave me a bag — the flayed hide of a nine-year ox —
and in it he bound the courses of the blustering winds:
for the son of Cronos made him steward of the winds,\nto still them or to rouse them, whichever he will.
In my hollow ship he lashed it fast with a shining cord
of silver, so that not the\nsmallest breath could slip past;
and for me he sent out the West Wind's breath to blow,\nto carry the ships and the men. But it was not to be
accomplished: we were destroyed by our own folly.
Nine days and nights alike we sailed on, and on the\ntenth our fathers' fields were rising into view —
so near, we could see men tending their fires.
Then sweet sleep came over me, worn out as I was:
all that time I had worked the\nship's sheet myself, yielding it
to no other companion, to bring us home the faster.
And the companions began to talk to one another,\nand said I was bringing home gold and silver for myself,
gifts of great-hearted Aeolus, Hippotas' son.
And thus would one of them say,\nwith a glance at his neighbor:
'Look at him — how loved he is, how honored,\namong all men, whatever city or land he comes to!
He carries out of Troy a mass of beautiful treasure,
his plunder — while we, who have accomplished\nthe same long road, come home with empty hands.
And now Aeolus, obliging him in friendship, has given him
this besides. Quick, then — let us see what is in it:
how much gold, how much silver the bag holds.'
So they talked, and the companions' evil counsel won.
They opened the bag — and all the winds burst out,
and the storm snatched them up\nat once and swept them seaward,
weeping, away from their fathers' land. And I,\nwaking, debated in my own blameless heart
whether to drop from the deck and drown in the sea\nor endure in silence and stay among the living.
I endured, and I stayed. Covering my head
I lay where I was; and the ships were\ncarried by the evil blast of the storm
back to the Aeolian island; and my companions groaned.
There we set foot on the mainland and drew water,
and the companions quickly took\ntheir meal beside the fast ships.
And when we had tasted food and drink,\nthen I took with me a herald and one companion
and went to the famous house of Aeolus.\nI found him feasting beside his wife and his children.
We came into the house and sat down by the doorposts
on the threshold; and they were\namazed at heart, and asked:
'How are you here, Odysseus? What evil power attacked you?
Surely we sent you off with all care, to reach
your fatherland and your house,\nand whatever place is dear to you.'
So they spoke; and I, grieving at heart, addressed them:
'My evil companions ruined me — they, and a pitiless\nsleep. But heal it, friends: the power is yours.'
So I spoke, plying them with soft words;\nand they fell silent. And the father answered:
'Out of this island — fast — you vilest thing alive!
It is against all right for me to harbor or to\nsend on his way a man the blessed gods detest.
Out! — since you come here hated by the deathless ones.'
So speaking he sent me from his house, groaning heavily.
From there we sailed on further, grieved at heart.
And the men's spirit was worn down by the grinding rowing —\nour own fault: no sending wind showed any more.
Six days and nights alike we sailed on,\nand on the seventh we came to Lamus' steep citadel —
Telepylus of the Laestrygonians,\nwhere herdsman hails herdsman:
the one driving in calls, and the one driving out answers.
There a sleepless man could have earned a double wage,\none herding cattle, one pasturing silvery sheep:
so close together are the paths of night and day.
There, when we came into the famous harbor —\na sheer cliff runs unbroken all around it, on both sides,
and jutting headlands, facing one another,\nthrust out at the mouth, and the entrance is narrow —
there all the others steered their curved ships in,
and moored them inside the hollow harbor, close together:
for no wave ever swelled in there, great or\nsmall, but a white calm lay all around it.
I alone held my black ship outside, there at\nthe edge, and made the cables fast to the rock;
and I climbed a broken lookout-height and stood there.
No works of oxen or of men showed anywhere;\nwe saw only smoke springing up from the land.
Then I sent companions ahead to learn what\nmen they were who ate bread upon this earth:
two men I chose, and sent a third with them as herald.
They went ashore and took a\nlevel road, by which the wagons
hauled timber down to the city from the high mountains,\nand before the city they met a girl drawing water,
the sturdy daughter of Laestrygonian Antiphates.
She had come down to the fair-flowing spring Artacia,\nfrom which they carried water to the town;
and they came up beside her and spoke to her,\nand asked who was king of these people, and whom he ruled;
and she pointed them at once to\nher father's high-roofed house.
But when they entered the famous\nhouse, they found his wife
huge as a mountain peak —\nand they were sick with horror at her.
She called famous Antiphates\nstraightway from the gathering-place —
her husband — and he plotted their wretched destruction:
he snatched up one of my companions\non the spot and made his meal of him,
and the other two sprang away\nand came flying to the ships.
Then he raised the war-cry\nthrough the city; and hearing it
the mighty Laestrygonians came thronging from every side,
thousands of them — not like men, but like the Giants.
From the cliffs they pelted us with man-heavy stones,\nand at once an evil din rose up along the ships —
the scream of dying men, the crunch of shattering hulls.
Spearing them like fish,\nthey carried home their loathsome meal.
While they were slaughtering those inside the deep\nharbor, I drew the sharp sword from beside my thigh
and cut the cables of my dark-blue-prowed ship,\nand quickly I roused my companions and ordered them
to fall to their oars and get us clear of the evil;
Gladly my ship fled out to open\nwater, away from the beetling
cliffs; but the others were destroyed there, all together.
From there we sailed on further, grieved at heart,\nglad to be out of death, having lost our dear companions.
And we came to the island of Aeaea; and there lived
Circe of the lovely braids, dread goddess with a\nmortal's voice, own sister of Aeetes the deadly-minded:
both born of Helios, who carries light to mortals,\nand of Perse their mother, whom Ocean fathered.
There we brought the ship silently to the shore
and into a harbor fit for ships;\nand some god was guiding us.
We stepped ashore there, and for two days and two nights
we lay, eating our hearts with\nweariness and pain together.
But when Dawn of the lovely braids brought the third\nday round, then I took my spear and my sharp sword
and went up quickly from the ship to a viewing-place,\nin hope of seeing men's works, or catching a voice.
I climbed a broken lookout-height and stood there,
and smoke showed to my eyes,\nrising from the wide-wayed earth
in Circe's halls, up through\nthe dense brush and the timber.
And I debated then in my mind and in my heart
whether to go and look, since I\nhad seen the fire-bright smoke.
And as I weighed it, this seemed to me the better way:
to go first to the fast ship and the shore of the sea,
give the companions their meal,\nand send them out to learn.
But when, on my way down, I was near the curved ship,\nthen some god took pity on me, alone as I was,
and sent a great high-antlered stag into my very path.
He was coming down to the river from his forest\npasture to drink, for the sun's force was heavy on him;
and as he stepped out I struck him on the spine, mid-back:
the bronze spear went clean through, and down he dropped\nin the dust with a cry, and the life flew from him.
I set my foot on him and drew the bronze spear out\nof the wound, and laid it down there on the ground
and left it; then I pulled brushwood and withies\nand plaited a rope, a fathom's length, well-twisted
all along, and bound together the feet of the huge beast,
and went down to the black ship\ncarrying him slung across my neck,
leaning on my spear: there was no carrying him on the\nshoulder with one hand — he was a very great beast.
I flung him down before the ship, and woke my companions\nwith gentle words, standing by each man in turn:
'Friends — for all our grief, we will not go down\nto the house of Hades before our destined day.
Come then, while there is food and drink in the fast ship,
let us think of eating, and not be worn away with hunger.'
So I spoke, and they quickly heeded my words:
they uncovered their heads there\nby the shore of the barren sea
and marveled at the stag: he was a very great beast.
And when they had had their joy of gazing,\nthey washed their hands and made the glorious feast ready.
So then all day long till the setting of the sun we\nsat feasting on meat past counting and sweet wine;
and when the sun went down and the dusk came on,\nthen we lay down to sleep on the surf-line of the sea.
When Dawn appeared, the early-born, with fingers of rose,
then I called an assembly, and spoke among them all:
'Hear my words, companions, for all your suffering.
Friends — we do not know where\nthe dark is, or where the dawn,
or where the sun that carries light\nto mortals goes under the earth,
or where he rises. Let us think, then — quickly —\nwhether any device is left us. I do not believe there is.
I climbed a broken lookout-height and saw an island,\nwreathed round with the boundless sea;
the island itself lies low,\nand in the middle of it my eyes
caught smoke, up through the dense brush and the timber.'
So I spoke, and their own hearts broke within them,\nremembering the deeds of Laestrygonian Antiphates
and the violence of the great-hearted man-eating Cyclops.
They wept aloud, letting the big tears fall —\nbut nothing came of all their mourning.
Then I counted off all my strong-greaved companions\ninto two bands, and gave each band a leader:
I led the one, and godlike Eurylochus the other.
We shook the lots quickly in a bronze helmet,\nand out jumped the lot of great-hearted Eurylochus.
So he set out, and with him two-and-twenty companions,\nweeping — and they left us behind in tears as well.
In a forest glen they found the house of Circe, built
of polished stones, in a place with a clear view all around;\nand around it were mountain wolves and lions —
creatures she herself had bewitched,\ngiving them evil drugs.
And these did not spring at the men, no:
they rose and fawned around them, waving their long tails.
As when dogs fawn around their\nmaster coming from a feast —
for he always carries home some sweet morsel for them —\nso the strong-clawed wolves and the lions fawned
around them; and they were terrified at\nthe sight of the dread huge creatures.
They stood in the gateway of\nthe goddess of the lovely hair,
and inside they heard Circe singing in a beautiful voice,
moving to and fro at her great\nimperishable loom — the weaving
goddesses do: fine-spun work, graceful and shining.
And Polites began to speak among them — a leader of men,
who of all my companions was closest and dearest to me:
'Friends — someone inside there, moving at a great loom,
is singing, beautifully — the whole floor hums with it —\ngoddess or woman. Quick, let us call out to her.'
So he spoke, and they lifted their voices and called.
And she came out at once, and opened the shining doors,
and invited them in; and all together, in their innocence,
they followed her. Only Eurylochus\nstayed behind, suspecting a snare.
She led them in and seated them on benches and chairs,
and stirred them a mixture:\ncheese and barley meal and pale honey
in Pramnian wine. And into the dish she blended
baleful drugs, to make them\nwholly forget their fathers' land.
And when she had served it and\nthey had drunk it down, at once
she struck them with her wand\nand penned them in the pigsties.
And they had the heads of pigs — the voice, the bristles,
the body — but their minds\nstayed steady, exactly as before.
So they were penned there weeping; and Circe threw\nthem acorns of oak and ilex, and cornel berries,
the things pigs eat, the wallowers on the ground.
But Eurylochus came running back to the fast black ship
to bring the news of the companions and their bitter fate.
And he could not get one word out, for all his straining —
struck to the heart with his great anguish; his eyes\nbrimmed full of tears, and his spirit was all lament.
But when we questioned him, all of us, in our amazement,
at last he told the destruction of the other companions:
'We went up through the brush,\nas you commanded, glorious Odysseus,
and in a forest glen we found a beautiful house, built
of polished stones, in a place\nwith a clear view all around.
And there someone at a great loom\nwas singing, clear and high —
goddess or woman. And they lifted their voices and called.
And she came out at once, and opened the shining doors,
and invited them in; and all together, in their innocence,
they followed her. But I stayed\nbehind, suspecting a snare.
And they vanished — all of them together. Not one of them
appeared again, though I sat a long time watching.'
So he spoke; and I slung my silver-studded sword
about my shoulders — the great\nbronze one — and my bow with it,
and ordered him to lead me back by the same way.
But he seized me with both hands, clasping my knees,\nand wailing he spoke winged words to me:
'Do not take me back there — Zeus-nurtured —\nagainst my will. Leave me here.
For I know it: you will not come\nback yourself, and you will not bring
one of your companions. No — with these men here,\nquickly, let us run: we may still escape the evil day.'
So he spoke, and I answered him and said:
'Eurylochus — stay here, then, where you are,\neating and drinking beside the hollow black ship.
But I am going. Hard necessity is on me.'
So speaking I went up from the ship and the sea.
But just as, threading the sacred glens, I was about\nto reach the great house of Circe of the many drugs,
there Hermes of the golden rod met me as I came\ntoward the house — in the likeness of a young man
with his first down on his lip,\nin the loveliest season of youth.
He clamped a hand on mine, and spoke a word, and named me:
'Where now, poor doomed man, alone along the heights,
a stranger to the country?\nYour companions there in Circe's house
are penned like pigs, packed in their hidden sties.
Is it to free them you are going?\nYou will not come back yourself,
I tell you: you will only stay there with the others.
But come — I will release you\nfrom the evil, I will save you.
Here. Take this good drug with you into Circe's house —\nit will keep the evil day away from your head.
And I will tell you all the deadly designs of Circe.
She will mix you a potion, and cast drugs into the dish;
but even so she will not have\npower to bewitch you: the good drug
I give you will not let her.\nAnd I will tell you everything.
The moment Circe strikes at you with her long wand,\nthat instant draw the sharp sword from beside your thigh
and go for Circe as though you meant to kill her.
She will be seized with terror, and invite you to her bed.
Do not, then, refuse the bed of the goddess —\nif you want her to free your companions and host you well —
but order her to swear the great oath of the blessed ones
that she is not planning some new evil against you:
lest she strip you naked and make\nyou a coward, an unmanned thing.'
So speaking, the slayer of Argus handed me the drug,\npulling it out of the ground, and showed me its nature:
at the root it was black, but its flower like milk.
The gods call it. And it is hard for mortal men to dig —\nbut the gods have power to do all things.
Then Hermes went away over the wooded island toward\nhigh Olympus; and I went on to the house of Circe,
and my heart ran dark with many things as I went.
I stopped at the doors of the goddess of the lovely hair,
and standing there I shouted;\nand the goddess heard my voice.
And she came out at once, and opened the shining doors,
and invited me in; and I followed her, grieved at heart.
She led me in and seated me on a silver-studded chair,
beautiful, cunningly worked, with a footstool for my feet,
and made me a potion in a golden cup, for me to drink,
and slipped a drug in it, with evil purpose in her heart.
And when she served it and I drank\nit off — and it did not bewitch me —
she struck me with her wand,\nand spoke a word, and named me:
'Off to the sty now. Lie down\nwith the rest of your companions.'
So she spoke; and I drew the\nsharp sword from beside my thigh
and went for Circe as though I meant to kill her.
And she shrieked, and ran under the blade, and seized\nmy knees, and wailing she spoke winged words to me:
'What man are you, and from where?\nWhere are your city and your parents?
Wonder holds me: you drank these\ndrugs and were not bewitched —
and no other man, no, not one, has withstood these drugs
once he drank them, once they\npassed the fence of his teeth.
The mind in your breast is proof against enchantment.
Surely you are Odysseus — the man of many turnings — whom
the golden-rodded slayer of\nArgus always told me would come,
on his way home from Troy in his fast black ship.
Come now — put your sword in its sheath, and let the\ntwo of us mount my bed together, so that mingled there
in the bed of love, we may come to trust one another.'
So she spoke, and I answered her and said:
'Circe — how can you bid me be gentle with you?
You who turned my companions into pigs in your own halls,\nand keep me here, and — scheming still — invite me
to your chamber, to climb into your bed, so that\nstripped naked I may be made a coward, an unmanned thing.
I will not consent to climb into your bed unless you\nbring yourself, goddess, to swear me the great oath
that you are not planning some new evil against me.'
So I spoke, and she swore it once, as I demanded.
And when she had sworn, and made an end of the oath,\nthen I mounted the surpassingly beautiful bed of Circe.
Meanwhile four handmaids were busy through the halls —\nthe serving-women who keep her house in order,
daughters of the springs and the groves and\nthe sacred rivers that flow out to the sea.
One of them threw beautiful covers over the chairs,\npurple above, with linen spread beneath;
another drew silver tables up before the\nchairs and set out golden baskets on them;
the third mixed honey-hearted wine, sweet wine,\nin a silver bowl, and set out golden cups;
and the fourth brought water and kindled a great\nfire under a huge cauldron, and the water warmed.
And when the water boiled in the bright bronze,\nshe set me in the tub and bathed me from the great cauldron,
tempering it to my liking,\npouring it over my head and shoulders,
until she had taken the heart-wasting\nweariness from my limbs.
And when she had bathed me and rubbed me richly with oil,
and thrown a beautiful cloak around me, and a tunic,\nshe led me in and seated me on a silver-studded chair,
beautiful, cunningly worked, with a footstool for my feet;
and a handmaid brought water for my hands in a pitcher,
a beautiful golden one, and poured it over a silver basin
for me to wash, and drew up a polished table beside me.
The grave housekeeper brought bread and set it before me,
laying out delicacies in plenty,\ngiving gladly of her store,
and pressed me to eat. But my heart was not in it:
I sat with my thoughts elsewhere,\nand my spirit boded evil.
And when Circe saw me sitting there, not reaching\nmy hands to the bread, gripped in a strong grief,
she came near, and spoke winged words to me:
'Why do you sit like this,\nOdysseus, like a man struck dumb,
eating your heart, and touching neither food nor drink?
Do you suspect some other snare? You have no cause\nto fear: I have already sworn you the strong oath.'
So she spoke, and I answered her and said:
'Circe — what man with any decency in\nhim could bear to taste of food and drink
before his companions were set free,\nand he saw them with his eyes?
If you press me in good faith to eat and drink,\nthen free them — let my eyes see my trusted companions.'
So I spoke, and Circe went out through the hall,\nwand in hand, and opened the doors of the sty,
and drove them out —\nin the shape of nine-year fattened hogs.
They stood there facing her; and she went\namong them anointing each with another drug;
and the bristles the baleful drug had grown on them —
the drug the lady Circe gave them —\ndropped from their limbs,
and they were men again — younger than they were before,\nfar more beautiful, and taller to the eye.
They knew me; and each man clung to my hands;\nand a passionate weeping came over us all, and the house
rang terribly around us; and the\ngoddess herself was moved to pity.
She came close beside me and spoke,\nshining among goddesses:
'Zeus-born son of Laertes, Odysseus of the many devices —\ngo now to your fast ship and the shore of the sea.
First of all, haul the ship up onto dry land,\nand stow your goods and all the tackle in the caves;
then come back yourself,\nand bring your trusted companions.'
So she spoke, and my proud heart consented.
I went my way to the fast ship and the shore of the sea,
and there by the fast ship I found my trusted companions\nin pitiful lamentation, letting the big tears fall.
As when farmyard calves around the herded cows that\ncome back to the dung-yard, filled with grazing,
all skip and frisk to meet them — the pens no\nlonger hold them, but lowing without pause they run
around their mothers: so those men,\nwhen their eyes took me in,
poured around me weeping. And to their hearts it felt
as if they had come to their fatherland, to their very\ntown in rugged Ithaca, where they were bred and born.
And wailing, they spoke winged words to me:
'At your return, Zeus-nurtured, we rejoice as if\nwe had come home to Ithaca, our fathers' land.
But come — tell the destruction of the other companions.'
So they spoke, and I answered with soft words:
'First of all, let us haul the ship up onto dry land,\nand stow our goods and all the tackle in the caves;
then bestir yourselves, all of you, and come with me,
so you may see our companions\nin the sacred halls of Circe,
eating and drinking: what they have never fails.'
So I spoke, and they quickly heeded my words.
Only Eurylochus tried to hold back all my companions,\nand lifting his voice he spoke winged words to them:
'Poor fools — where are we going?\nWhy do you hanker after these evils —
to go down into Circe's hall, who will turn\nevery one of us into pigs or wolves or lions
to guard her great house for her — and guard it we must —
the way the Cyclops did his work, when our companions
came to his inner yard,\nand the reckless Odysseus with them:
it was that man's blind folly killed them too.'
So he spoke; and I turned it over in my mind —
whether to draw the long-edged\nsword from beside my thick thigh,
strike off his head and bring it down in the dust,
kinsman by marriage though he was,\nand a close one. But my companions
held me back with honeyed words, this one and that one:
'Zeus-born — this man, if you command it, we will\nleave here by the ship, to stay and guard the ship;
lead the rest of us to the sacred house of Circe.'
So speaking they went up from the ship and the sea;\nand Eurylochus was not left behind by the hollow ship —
he followed.
Meanwhile, in her house,\nCirce had bathed the other companions
with kind care, and rubbed them richly with oil,\nand thrown about them fleecy cloaks and tunics,
and we found them all feasting well in the halls.
And when the men saw one another,\nface to face, and knew each other,
they wept and lamented, and the house rang round them.
And she came close beside me and\nspoke, shining among goddesses:
'No more of this swelling lament now. I know it myself —\nall you have suffered on the fish-filled sea,
all the harm lawless men have done you on dry land.
Come now: eat your food, and drink your wine,\nuntil you gather back the spirit in your breasts
that was yours when you first left your fathers' land\nof rugged Ithaca. Now you are withered, spiritless,
forever brooding on the misery\nof your wandering — your hearts
never in the feast, for truly you have suffered much.'
So she spoke, and our proud hearts consented.
So there, day after day, for the full round of a year,\nwe sat feasting on meat past counting and sweet wine.
But when the year was out,\nand the seasons turned in their wheel,
as the months waned and the long days came round,\nthen my trusted companions called me out, and said:
'You are possessed! It is time\nto remember your fatherland —
if it is truly decreed that you be saved, and come\nto your high-roofed house and your own fatherland.'
So they spoke, and my proud heart consented.
So then all day long till the setting of the sun we\nsat feasting on meat past counting and sweet wine;
and when the sun went down and the dusk came on,\nthe men lay down to sleep through the shadowy halls,
but I climbed into the surpassingly beautiful bed of Circe
and clasped her knees in supplication;\nand the goddess heard my voice.
And lifting my voice I spoke winged words to her:
'Circe — make good now the promise that you made me,\nto send me home. My spirit strains for it already,
and my companions' too: they wear my heart away,\nmourning around me whenever you are elsewhere.'
So I spoke, and she answered at once,\nshining among goddesses:
'Zeus-born son of Laertes, Odysseus of the many devices:
stay no longer in my house against your will.
But there is another journey you must\naccomplish first: you must go down
to the house of Hades and dread Persephone\nto consult the ghost of Theban Tiresias,
the blind seer, whose mind stands fast:
to him, even dead, Persephone has granted understanding —
to him alone the power of thought.\nThe rest flit past as shadows.
So she spoke, and my heart broke within me,\nand I wept, sitting there on the bed; my heart
had no more will to live and see the light of the sun.
But when I had had my fill of weeping and writhing,\nthen I answered her with words, and said:
'Circe — and who will be pilot on that voyage?
No man ever yet reached Hades in a black ship.'
So I spoke, and she answered at once,\nshining among goddesses:
'Zeus-born son of Laertes, Odysseus of the many devices:
let no lack of a pilot at the ship concern you.
Set up the mast, spread the white sails open,\nand sit: the breath of the North Wind will carry her.
But when in your ship you have\ncrossed the stream of Ocean,
there is a scrub shore there,\nand the groves of Persephone —
tall black poplars, and willows\nthat shed their fruit unripened,
Beach the ship there, on Ocean's deep-eddying edge,\nand go on yourself into the dank house of Hades.
There into Acheron pour Pyriphlegethon and Cocytus,\nwhich is a branch broken off the water of Styx;
and there is a rock,\nat the meeting-roar of the two rivers.
Draw close to it there, hero, as I command you,\nand dig a pit about a cubit's measure this way and that,
and around it pour a drink-offering to all the dead —
first with milk and honey mingled, then with sweet wine,
the third time with water;\nand sprinkle white barley over it.
And entreat, over and over,\nthe strengthless heads of the dead:
vow that, come to Ithaca, you will offer in your halls
a barren heifer, your best,\nand heap the pyre with good things;
and to Tiresias, apart, alone, you will sacrifice a ram
all black, the one that stands out from all your flocks.
Then, when with prayers you have entreated the glorious\ntribes of the dead, sacrifice a ram and a black ewe,
bending their heads toward Erebus —\nbut turn yourself away,
facing the river's streams. And there will come,\nin crowds, the souls of the dead who are gone.
Then rouse your companions, and command them
to flay the sheep that lie there slaughtered by the\npitiless bronze, and burn them, and pray to the gods —
to mighty Hades and dread Persephone.
And you: draw the sharp sword from beside your thigh
and sit, and do not let the strengthless heads of the\ndead come near the blood before you question Tiresias.
And quickly then the seer will come, leader of peoples,
and he will tell you the road,\nand the measures of your journey,
and your homecoming — how you\nshall go over the fish-filled sea.'
So she spoke; and at once Dawn\nof the golden throne came on.
She dressed me then in my clothes, a cloak and a tunic,
and she, the nymph, put on a great silver-shining mantle,
fine-woven and graceful, and cast about her waist a belt,
beautiful, golden, and set a veil on her head above.
And I went through the halls and roused my companions\nwith gentle words, standing by each man in turn:
'No more lying now, drowsing in sweet sleep.
Let us go: the lady Circe has shown me the way.'
So I spoke, and their proud hearts consented.
But not even from there could I\nbring my companions off unharmed.
There was one, Elpenor, the youngest of all —\nno great fighter in war, no steady mind on him —
who had lain down apart from his\ncompanions in the sacred house of Circe,
heavy with wine, wanting the cool air.
Hearing the noise and stir of his companions moving,
he leapt up all at once — and forgot, in his fuddled wits,\nto come back down again by the long ladder;
he fell headlong from the roof, and his neck snapped\nfrom the spine; and his soul went down to Hades.
And as my men were setting out I spoke among them:
'You think, no doubt, that you are going home, to your own
dear fatherland. But Circe has\nmarked out another road for us:
to the house of Hades and dread Persephone,\nto consult the ghost of Theban Tiresias.'
So I spoke, and their own hearts broke within them:
they sat down right where they were,\nand wailed, and tore their hair —
but nothing came of all their mourning.
And while we walked to the fast ship and the shore\nof the sea, grieving, letting the big tears fall,
Circe meanwhile had gone down, and beside the\nblack ship had tethered a ram and a black ewe —
slipping past us with ease. Who could see a god\nagainst the god's will, moving here or there?
